item.title: Reading Between the Lines
item.content:encoded:
I went ahead and added a collapsible form to the level five clearance portion of the article, hopefully that will make it flow a little better for some of those who don't think it does. As far as all of the expungements go, I think I am actually able to read between some of the lines. I know that it's not usually done this way in order for each of our imaginations to run wild so that everybody has their own interpretation, but I'm going to go ahead and put down what I think most of the expungements are, at least the important ones, including the one at the end in the final paragraph.

Redactions
Hide

For example, one ██-hour study of what seemed to be a significant cipher proved to translate into a long and painstakingly thorough list of extremely unofficial synonyms for a human █████.

*sniggering*

…strings of letters, [DATA EXPUNGED] incomprehensible words, sounds that cannot be produced by any known animal that continue for extended amounts of time (███ unconfirmed languages have been distinguished to date, ██ of which are reoccurring), monologues, nursery rhymes, [REDACTED] leading to speculation as to whether or not the narrator is in fact human, etc.

This actually confused me as to what the difference is between 'redacted' and 'data expunged' is in these articles. Aside from that, I believe that the data expunged portion is merely Foundation sensitive information, such as GOI information or just simply information on other SCPs. The redacted portion maybe some piece of crucial information based on what is said after; ie. some horribly monstrous noise or even a digital or computationally created noise. These would logically lead to some doubt if the narrator was human or not.

…and a handful of [sounds believed to be heard by victims of SCP-217 or 2510] Morse code, [Synchronized(?)] human screaming, various computer programming languages, every known language on earth (including, in one incident, Pig Latin), [Distorted humming/other displaced or arbitrary noises] possibly of biological origin, condescending laughter, music, music played backwards, music [from SCP-012], conversations that have evidently been recorded ranging from [White House/The Kremlin/The Vadican/Parliament, etc.] significant and extensively protected area to what was most likely an average household, discussing what grocery supplies to buy from the supermarket, static, ambient soundtracks, etc.

It wasn't until I got to this that I realized what all of you meant by tone. Even after each expungement and reduction there should be a comma, especially if that expungement or reduction does not have anything to do with the phrase listed directly afterward. I feel that that was forgotten for some of these and for others it was intended, making it all the more confusing and hard to follow the flow.

Speaking into SCP-270 has no effect on SCP-270-1. Currently disputed, refer to Incident-270-█ in which [Agent/Researcher █, made a passive comment toward the narrator, at which time he was met with the response, "Well, that's YOUR opinion!"]

…or however creepy/tame you want it to be.

[Personnel assigned believe there to be a sentient(?)] nature of SCP-270, (that) this is exactly what it wants, if certain people are to be trusted [to be in contact with or exchange possible false (or worse) information between SCP-270 and 05-██, would be] disconcerting to said O5 member. [Dialing-out/Dialogues is/are] not, in fact, a method of safe communication between unknown entities, as originally hypothesized, but rather [a means for 270's operators to gather information/a tactic to falsify Foundation intelligence].

I know this is reaching a tad, but I believe this to be around what the original author was trying to get across. That the SCP may or may not basically be a ploy to confuse and thin-out The Foundation's resources.

So…wow. After making this post I totally see what all of you mean when you talk about the tone or the flow. There are SO many █s and reductions and expungements, that it becomes difficult to tell the difference between them and follow the flow. In the collapsible, I also mention the possibility of misplaced or left out commas which I just can't ignore it. If this thing ever needs a tone change I'd be happy to help.

But, in the end, I actually can't get over how much I like the concept for this thing. I think that most of us here like it because it would get to most of us as well in real life. It's always, in my opinion, much more scary to get half-truths than full ones, and I feel that this is exactly what this thing is doing. Giving us information when it's convenient. +1 despite everything.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
Downvote, partially because there are just too many redactions and expungements in places they don't seem necessary. I feel like the two paragraphs that describe what comes over the line could be condensed to one, and just remove all the redactions from there. Redactions seem to be getting used improperly or too much in this one.

And I know it's a bit older, but I just don't like the idea of there being so many "items what can't be moved" out there. I mean, even if there's only a few dozen things like that, some of these items would start getting noticed. Maybe this was one of the first ones or something, but that little trope bugs me sometimes.

Picking some nits
Hide Amo's nitpicking

I don't really get why the population information where it was found was important at all, especially since pretty much all the details are black-boxed anyway.

Somewhere between 100 and 999 people somehow fitting inside a fake farmhouse? Come on, that needs to be changed if the facility is going to remain a farmhouse facade. Or at least mention there's a big ol' underground facility under the farm so that even 100 people doesn't seem absolutely ludicrous to have stationed there.

Is "power cord" technically the right word? With a phone like that, shouldn't it be "phone cord"?

The line about sounds coming "from no known animal"… So it's a piano? Digital autotuning of Mary J Blige? An alien gargling mouthwash? That's so vague it doesn't make sense being in there, imo.

"Military time" being explicitly mentioned (even though it's blacked out anyway). Just… why?

As it is impossible to determine how useful portions of SCP-270-1 will be, personnel are advised to choose whatever segments of SCP-270-1 they deem to be most promising.

How the heck are they supposed to "deem" what's most promising when it says right before that it is "impossible to determine" what's useful? If it means what's most promising as far as "most likely to be deciphered", then it needs to be reworded to make that clear. It's just a weird statement as is.

And then the part where the computer can't decode any of it because reasons. Let's be serious here… There's no way they are writing down everything coming out as it's happening, so it must be recorded, right? I think we can all agree that's the case, yes? Why can't a computer parse the information, then? They must be storing the recordings somehow, and I don't see shelves upon shelves of cassette tapes making any sense.

If that computer can't decode everything, okay. That's fine, makes sense, and prevents computers from being the deus ex machina of this SCP's challenge. But decommissioning the computer specifically built to decode the nonsense coming out of SCP-270 because it can't do what people with a pencil and paper have apparently been doing since the thing was found? I need a good reason for that to be the case.

And the last thing I have to say is somewhat minor… Have they tried attaching another phone to the cord? Does the "broadcast" continue under that circumstance? If it does, I feel like the cord should maybe be designated SCP-270 instead of the phone. In other words, that small test should maybe be added to confirm that the phone itself, or the phone and cord together, is the scip. That, or the cord is hardwired to the phone, so there's no RJ45 jack on the thing? (I think RJ45 is the right type of plug.)

Predictions with a twist. This if kind of like 909, but more unsettling, and is different enough, IMO.
